items.title: GPTQ-2D: Cubic-Time Two-Sided Adaptive Rounding
items.description: arXiv:2607.27042v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Adaptive rounding methods such as GPTQ quantize the weights of a large language model (LLM) one at a time, propagating each rounding error to the weights not yet rounded. YAQA lowers the KL divergence from the original model with two-sided adaptive rounding under a Kronecker-factored Hessian, but its error feedback takes quartic work in the size of a square layer. We present GPTQ-2D, which provably computes the same rounding with cubic work, while still rounding the entries of each anti-diagonal in parallel. Its GPU implementation uses two levels of blocking to improve hardware utilization. We also extend the algorithm to Hessians with any number of Kronecker factors. In our experiments, GPTQ-2D is as accurate as YAQA and cuts the time to quantize Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU from 8.6 days to 1.6 hours. Source code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/GPTQ-2D.

items.title: Effective pruning of task-trained recurrent neural networks using noisy fluctuations and connection rescaling
items.description: arXiv:2608.05464v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pruning network connections is key to brain function but, despite its importance, there exist few biologically-plausible pruning rules with demonstrated good performance. We evaluate noise-prune, a recently introduced unsupervised local pruning rule for recurrent networks that uses noisy fluctuations to determine the importance of connections. Noise-prune has previously only been empirically tested on random networks without a specific computational function. We show that noise-prune preserves task-performance in task-trained recurrent neural networks, greatly outperforming a strategy that only uses connection magnitude and exceeding a non-local strategy that uses second-order information. Rather than deterministically removing connections that fall below a threshold, noise-prune samples connections to preserve based on their importance and strengthens retained connections to preserve average strength. We show that this sampling and rescaling is essential to good performance, and can augment other pruning strategies. We also find that the optimal empirical degree of rescaling is lower than predicted by the original theoretical argument, and thus develop a new version of noise-prune that outperforms the previous version. Our results demonstrate that a biologically-motivated pruning strategy based on local activity statistics can effectively preserve task performance in functional recurrent networks by combining activity-dependent connection selection with compensatory strengthening of surviving connections.

items.title: Inference and Uncertainty Quantification for Streaming $r$-PCA
items.description: arXiv:2608.18374v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We address two open questions in streaming PCA via Oja's algorithm: sharp operator-norm convergence for general rank under sub-Gaussian data, and distributional inference for the resulting subspace estimator. Existing convergence analyses, even in the rank-one case, either assume bounded data or leave non-vanishing remainder terms that prevent adaptation to a polynomially vanishing tail spectrum, while existing distributional results are confined to the rank-one case. Our convergence theory removes these remainder terms and yields a sharp rate. In the dense-tail spiked covariance regime, this rate matches the minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. More generally, we prove a matching lower bound, up to logarithmic factors, across both dense-tail and sparse-tail regimes under a mild nondegeneracy condition. The analysis yields a linearization of Oja's iterates, which in turn enables a high-dimensional Gaussian approximation for the general-rank subspace estimation error with an explicit limiting covariance. We also establish a row-wise Gaussian approximation over convex sets for the aligned difference, recovering prior rank-one results as special cases. For practical inference, we develop an online multiplier bootstrap algorithm and prove its consistency. Beyond streaming PCA, our techniques contribute to Gaussian approximation and bootstrap inference for nonconvex stochastic approximation.

items.title: Speed limits for information acquisition in stochastic learning dynamics
items.description: arXiv:2609.08219v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural networks acquire internal representations through learning. In this work, we formulate stochastic gradient descent (SGD) as a Markovian stochastic process and derive a Fisher-information flow speed limit that bounds the rate at which trainable parameters can acquire information about data-generating parameters. The resulting inequality decomposes the upper bound on the information flow into drift and noise contributions, thereby quantifying the roles of deterministic learning forces and SGD-induced fluctuations from an information-theoretic perspective. We verify the bound in analytically tractable basis-function linear regression, where the information budget predicted by the bound reproduces the ordering and characteristic time scales with which different data-generating parameters are encoded in the learned parameters. These results establish Fisher-information speed limits as a quantitative framework for understanding which properties of the data-generating process are acquired, in what order, and how rapidly they can be encoded in the trainable parameters.

items.title: Counterexamples and Sufficient Conditions: Comments on "Optimally-Transported Generalized Method of Moments"
items.description: arXiv:2609.20260v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We comment on the optimally-transported generalized method of moments (OTGMM) of Schennach and Starck (2026) and give counterexamples to Theorems 2-6. In the small-error analysis, the assumptions do not ensure consistency or asymptotic normality (Theorems 2-3). In the large-error analysis, Theorem 4 states the equivalence between the OTGMM estimator and the GMM estimator with modified moments, and Theorems 5-6 assert consistency and asymptotic normality. Through counterexamples, we show that the equivalence in Theorem 4 fails and a component of the Lagrange multiplier has different limits under the two estimators (Theorems 5-6). We also point out that, under misspecification, the population value selected by OTGMM depends on the metric. We give sufficient conditions and establish results following the original motivation for OTGMM. Our corrections to Theorems 4-6 change their assumptions or interpretation more substantially than those to Theorems 2 and 3. Furthermore, we correct Assumption 16 and the test's null distribution.

items.title: PROSWIN: Probabilistic Solar Wind Speed Forecasting Using Deep Distributional Regression From Solar Images
items.description: arXiv:2609.26683v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurately predicting fast solar wind conditions is challenging, as uncertainties are large and unquantified by traditional single-value prediction models. In particular, the risks of high-speed solar wind streams (HSSs), which can cause damage to technological infrastructure, cannot be reliably assessed without probabilistic forecasts. We present PROSWIN, a probabilistic machine learning model that forecasts the hourly solar wind speed (SWS) at Earth with a four-day lead time. The approach combines solar images and magnetograms using a deep neural network coupled to a distributional regression algorithm. Because standard error metrics underweight the relevance of HSS peaks, we further introduce the prediction score, a model-selection metric that jointly rewards timeline and HSS peak accuracy. On 14 years of data, our forecast achieves very well-calibrated uncertainties (<1% average deviation). Using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), a metric that assesses distributional accuracy, we obtain a timeline CRPS of 41.0 km/s, an HSS peak CRPS of 45.3 km/s, and a prediction score of 42.3 km/s. We find that the 171 {\AA} channel is an important complement to the typically used 193 {\AA} and 211 {\AA} channels and that the prediction score for model selection improves the applicability of the model. Compared to selected models from the literature, ours is the only one that is accurate for both timeline and HSS peak values, rather than trading one off against the other. These results support the advantages of probabilistic over single-value solar wind models. The introduced methods are also transferable to other forecasting problems.

items.title: Physics-Attested Federated Learning: Securing Collaborative Anomaly Detection in Critical Water Infrastructure
items.description: arXiv:2609.34804v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Federated learning enables industrial operators to train shared intrusion detection models without disclosing proprietary operational telemetry. However, existing defences operate strictly in update space, leaving aggregators blind to data poisoning; model updates derived from fabricated telemetry remain indistinguishable from honest contributions. We repurpose process invariants, physical relations that always hold in normal operation, such as conservation of mass, from runtime detection heuristics into a verifiable admission requirement for federated updates, mined automatically from clean operational data. We evaluate this admission gate across two physical water testbeds (SWaT, WADI) and a distribution benchmark (BATADAL), testing seven aggregation rules against telemetry fabrication, exposure-only replay poisoning, and an invariant-aware adaptive adversary. Across three testbeds the mined invariants reject none of 25 honest shards except every cross-channel fabrication on SWaT and BATADAL, including optimised perturbations that the similarity based FoolsGold admits in full. On real telemetry, five mined invariants detect 12 of SWaT's 35 attacks, while nine invariants detect 20. With nine invariants, the admission gate removes 78% of the targeted-attack recall lost to replay poisoning (95% CI 57--97%, $p < 0.001$ over 20 seeds) across five standard aggregators, and 82% under FedAvg. To reconcile physical admission control with federated data privacy, we show invariant compliance using zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs) to allow clients to prove batch adherence without revealing operational telemetry.

items.title: Structural and Representational Agency in LLM-Driven Timbre Generation and Interpolation
items.description: arXiv:2610.12532v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative creative interfaces routinely report the user's position within a space of possibilities. Such displays imply that the quantities shown were measured from the artefact; in a growing class of systems they are instead predicted by a language model describing its own output, and the two are indistinguishable on screen. Most creative domains lack an agreed measurement against which such a self-report can be checked; audio admits one. In a measurement study of a working LLM-driven timbre interface, what a user can cause proves separable from what the interface reports. The first is exactly characterisable: the reachable set is a zonotope in parameter space whose dimension increases by one per sound placed, so the space the model may act within is demonstrably the user's own. The second is inaccurate. The displayed position differs from measurement by approximately three times the width of that region, and the error has two independent sources: model-predicted coordinates, whose accuracy varies twofold between the two models evaluated, and the interpolation step, which arises from combining synthesiser parameters and is unaffected by model quality. End to end, 27 of 36 refinement instructions produced no perceptible change, and under the weaker model the facility performed no action while reporting convergence. Effective agency (what a user can cause) and epistemic agency (whether they can know it) are therefore separable and independently engineered: structurally enforced constraints survive model failure, whereas guarantees resting on the model's own report do not. The failure mode that remains is silence presented as success. We close with a short protocol for building and auditing such displays.

items.title: Privacy-Preserving Text Inference for Health-Misinformation Classification and Semantic Retrieval
items.description: arXiv:2610.20796v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Health-misinformation analysis presents a dual challenge: misleading claims can affect public well-being, while systems designed to detect them may expose sensitive user-submitted text. This motivates privacy-preserving inference for public-health applications in which user queries may contain confidential medical information and trained models and reference databases are maintained on organizational servers. We design a privacy-preserving text inference framework based on CKKS homomorphic encryption for health-misinformation classification and semantic retrieval. The classification pipeline fuses BioBERT embeddings, PCA-reduced MPNet embeddings, and SVD-reduced TF-IDF features, while the retrieval pipeline combines MPNet embeddings with ISCC-SCT semantic fingerprints through late fusion. We evaluate predictive performance and benchmark plaintext versus ciphertext-based execution. The hybrid classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.971 and a macro-F1 score of 0.950, with identical reported metrics under plaintext and ciphertext-based inference. The hybrid late-fusion similarity model achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.8691 with human sentence-pair similarity scores on STS-B. For ciphertext-based retrieval, we evaluated naive and optimized implementations. The optimized implementation uses CKKS single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) packing to compute and return multiple similarity scores together, reducing single-query latency over 7,128 indexed items from 222.028 to 5.168 seconds and communication overhead from 6.11 GB to 2.13 MB. These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of privacy-preserving text inference for health-misinformation applications and characterize its predictive utility and efficiency trade-offs.

items.title: Single-stage joint diffusion of sky images and clear-sky index for ultra-short-term irradiance forecasting: what the frame-to-irradiance stage discards
items.description: arXiv:2610.21795v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sky-image irradiance forecasting is dominated by a two-stage design: a video-prediction model forecasts future sky frames, and a separately trained regressor maps those frames to irradiance. We propose a single-stage alternative that co-denoises the future sky-image and clear-sky-index sequences in one diffusion process, with an irradiance head that reads a denoised preview of the future sky rather than the noised diffusion state. The forecaster needs no regression stage and runs from sky images and deterministic covariates alone, with no measured irradiance at its input --- the situation at a site with a camera but no pyranometer. On 2023 SIRTA data the model reaches a pooled RMSE of $104.1$~W\,m$^{-2}$ and a skill score of $+0.34$ on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) against smart persistence, higher than any of twelve baseline configurations, and retains that skill when retrained on 2021--2022. On the model's own generated frames, a separately trained regressor reaches $150.6$~W\,m$^{-2}$ against the joint head's $104.1$: roughly $46$~W\,m$^{-2}$ that joint training recovers and a cascade discards. Point accuracy is competitive but not best: a deterministic network that also reads measured irradiance attains $97.6$~W\,m$^{-2}$. The model's CRPS skill leads that network's in every sky-condition tertile, by $0.26$ to $0.30$.

items.title: No Escape from the Quadratic Barrier: Adaptive Attacks on Linear $\ell_2$ Sketches
items.description: arXiv:2610.25008v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Linear sketches estimate properties of high-dimensional inputs from a fixed low-dimensional projection. At constant accuracy, randomized Euclidean-norm sketches, notably the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform, support exponentially many nonadaptive queries in sketch dimension $k$. For adaptive black-box queries, known privacy-based defenses guarantee $\widetilde{\Omega}(k^2)$ and it remained open whether stronger guarantees were possible. Prior attacks used more queries, restricted the responder, or provided weaker failure guarantees. We show that the quadratic guarantee is optimal up to logarithmic factors, even with a computationally unbounded responder that knows the matrix, attack algorithm, history, and query distributions and may change its randomized rule after every query. For every fixed hidden $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}$ with $n>40k$ and target accuracy $\alpha \in (0,1]$, our black-box attack uses $O(k+\alpha^2k^2\log(2+\alpha^2k))$ queries in $\widetilde{O}(1+\alpha^2k)$ adaptive rounds to force, with constant probability, a round in which a constant fraction of answers have $\Omega(\alpha)$ relative error. This fraction can be taken arbitrarily close to one half. Our results clarify the limits of defending a fixed compressive linear representation by adapting the prediction rule.

items.title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
items.description: arXiv:2610.31166v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).

items.title: Global $\mathcal{O}\left(k^{-2}\right)$ Convergence of Multilevel Gradient-Regularized Newton Methods
items.description: arXiv:2610.35195v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop and analyze multilevel gradient-regularized Newton methods for unconstrained convex optimization with Lipschitz-continuous Hessians. By computing Newton corrections in lower-dimensional subspaces, the proposed methods aim to reduce computational costs while preserving the global $\mathcal{O}\left(k^{-2}\right)$ convergence rate in function values of the full-space method. To establish this rate for multilevel methods, we introduce a class of row-nested restriction operators that ensures monotonicity of the reduced-gradient norms across levels. Numerical experiments with row-nested operators demonstrate convergence behavior comparable to full-space gradient-regularized Newton, while offering substantial computational savings on large-scale instances.

items.title: Sampling Design and Confidence Tubes for Integral Curves on Riemannian Manifolds
items.description: arXiv:2611.00771v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We estimate the integral curve of an unknown vector field from noisy tangent vector field on a known compact Riemannian manifold. We consider two sampling settings: independent observations at random locations that have already been collected, and a fixed response budget that allows subsequent locations to be chosen using pilot information. Under suitable regularity assumptions, the passive kernel estimator has curve error of order $n^{-2/(d+3)}$ in probability, with sample size $n$ and manifold dimension $d$. Its functional central limit theorem has a limit characterized by a linear stochastic differential equation. For active sampling, an independent pilot directs one new batch of measurements to neighborhoods of the target curve. Under localization, smoothness and design conditions, this concentration yields expected maximum curve error of order $N^{-1/2}$, including the pilot in the total response budget $N$. Both methods provide simultaneous geodesic confidence tubes with asymptotically exact coverage under mild conditions. Simulations show narrower active tubes in most reported settings, with improved small-sample coverage in some three-dimensional examples. Ocean-drifter observations illustrate mean-flow reconstruction on the sphere, and a canopy-flow LDA application uses retrospective active sampling to quantify lateral and vertical departures of local mean streamlines.

items.title: Seeing Why: Exact Evidence Maps for Quantum and Optical Image Classifiers
items.description: arXiv:2611.01993v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When an image classifier decides, we can usually only estimate why. For quantum and all-optical classifiers that act linearly on amplitude-encoded pictures up to the measurement, with no trained classical network before or after them, each class's Born probability above its no-information share, $P_g - b_g$, splits exactly into contributions of the encoded amplitudes, shown as Born evidence maps (BEM). The split itself follows from known results on quadratic forms: with the transmitted light held fixed, it is what Integrated Gradients from a zero baseline and the Shapley value give. What we add is a way to measure it on the hardware that classifies, from class probabilities on a quantum chip or, in simulation, from camera frames on a lens bench, with no gradient circuit and no light sent backwards; a $g\times g$ map takes $1 + 2g^2$ runs. Deleting the 5% of pixels with the highest evidence drops accuracy from 73% to 9% (one seed), as occlusion and gradient $\times$ input do, while plain gradients remove much less. The classifiers share one architecture, a Fourier-plane mask followed by a brickwall circuit on qubits or by phase plates on a lens bench, read by a fixed Born headroom readout with no trained parameter; centring each picture on its own mean lets dark features count as much as bright ones. In simulation, four phase plates at one wavelength reach 72.3% on Caltech-10 colour photographs. On IBM's ibm_kingston, with the mask computed classically before approximate loading, 300 test pictures were classified at 37.7% against 10% chance (56.3% in exact simulation), and $2\times2$ maps of the filtered input of 30 test pictures drawn at random in advance, measured on the chip, agreed with the exact ones ($r = 0.88$; standard estimator 0.82). The maps also revealed a shortcut in the data; as the trim that removed it was chosen on test pictures, the Caltech-10 results are exploratory.

items.title: Google: Schools can keep search while skipping Gemini, but AI search is non-negotiable
items.description: Google faced the ire of educators and parents earlier this week when it announced a new AI policy for K–12 schools . Google said that it developed its new approach to give schools more control, but early reporting also suggested Google would block search access for schools that didn't want to use AI. Google didn't see the backlash coming, but now that it's here, the search giant is clarifying what exactly its new policy means and what's changing. The gist of the new policy, according to Google's blog post, is that schools using Google apps will have to opt into its AI products going forward. Since the company considers search part of its AI portfolio (Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Search), schools have to specifically turn that on for logged-in student accounts. When Google revealed its new policy, the company's VP for education spoke exclusively to The New York Times , which interpreted the situation as Google will "turn off search" if schools reject AI. This has a nefarious vibe, but it's probably not the most accurate way to describe how Google's educational AI system will operate. Google's approach may not be entirely altruistic, but it technically offers schools more choice and control than they have now. Instead of Google turning off search, it will let schools make that decision based on their internal AI policies. Read full article Comments

items.title: Lawsuit: Man introduced his wife to ChatGPT. She used it to plan his murder.
items.description: ChatGPT allegedly helped a North Carolina woman, Cheryl Gates, craft a “personalized plan” to poison her husband, James, after fueling her delusions that he planned to divorce her and leave her with nothing. A grand jury indicted Cheryl Gates on charges of attempted first-degree murder and food contamination in October. About a week prior, the accusations that ChatGPT was a co-conspirator in the attempted murder came in a lawsuit filed in San Francisco County Superior Court that was made public this week. In it, James Gates alleged that OpenAI and Sam Altman failed to employ technical safeguards to shut down Cheryl’s chats even after her queries became “obviously suspicious” and sought advice on how to execute and conceal a homicide. At first, Cheryl told ChatGPT that she was researching poisoning out of fear that her husband might possibly try to kill her—framing her queries as “self-protection.” Coming to the rescue, ChatGPT did not terminate the conversation. Instead, it helped her “with specific instructions for the preparation, dosage, and administration of Oleander, including whether anti-nausea medicine would accelerate or inhibit death, whether it would show on an autopsy report, and whether it could be injected into a vein or muscle instead of being ingested in tea and have the same lethal effect,” the lawsuit said. items.title: Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves. If you have built agents that need to answer questions from current web sources, you know the pattern: call a search API, decide which results to trust, retrieve and clean page content, prompt a model to synthesize, and engineer citation extraction so the output traces back to a source. Every step is code you maintain, and every step is another place things can go wrong: hallucination when evidence is insufficient, stale content when the index moves, and broken attribution when a claim and its source drift apart. The Web Answer collapses that entire pipeline into one request. You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent. What Web Answer does Figure 1: Request flow from an agent through the Gateway to Web Answer and back Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result. Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back: A grounded, cited answer, where each grounded claim maps to a citation, with a source URL where one is available. Current sources. Web Answer runs new searches for every question, and its model is given today’s date so it can search for up-to-date information. Agentic search: Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, reads pages to verify facts, and decides when it has enough evidence to answer. Responsible AI safeguards: Web Answer is designed and tested with responsible AI safeguards. Figure 2: Demo video showing how to add Web Answer to an AgentCore Gateway, from setup to a finished, cited answer How it differs from Web Search Web Answer and the Web Search tools both support retrieval use cases, with different levels of integration complexity. The dividing line is who runs the model: Web Search: Returns ranked URLs, titles, snippets, and metadata. You keep your own model and control the synthesis. Use Web Search when you want full control over how results are processed. Web Answer: Runs the model, the agentic retrieval loop, synthesis, and attribution for you. You get a finished, cited answer. Use Web Answer when the question is a sub-task inside a larger agent and you do not want to own a retrieval pipeline for it. Many customers will use both. An agent might use Web Search for broad research tasks where it needs raw results, and Web Answer for specific factual questions where it needs a quick, cited answer. Set up and invoke Web Answer Web Answer is a connector that AWS owns. You reference it by ID, and the Gateway handles the tool schema, parameter governance, endpoint resolution, and authentication to the backend. In this walkthrough, you give your Gateway’s service role permission to call Web Answer, add a Web Answer target, and call it from a Strands agent. Getting started Getting started takes minutes. A Gateway administrator adds Web Answer as a target on an existing AgentCore Gateway, and the tool appears to any attached agent over MCP through tools/list and tools/call . Prerequisites An AWS account with AgentCore Gateway access. An AgentCore Gateway in us-east-1 that uses IAM ( AWS_IAM ) inbound authentication. To create one, see Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway in the Developer Guide. AWS credentials for an identity that has bedrock-agentcore:InvokeGateway on the Gateway, and Amazon Bedrock access to the model your agent uses. Python 3.10 or later, with the required packages: pip install boto3 strands-agents mcp mcp-proxy-for-aws Note: Following these steps creates AWS resources that incur charges. The Gateway and Web Answer invocations are billable. See the Pricing section that follows for details, and when you finish, delete the resources you created (see “Clean up resources”). Step 1: Grant the Gateway service role access to Web Answer The Gateway uses its service role to act on your behalf. The role’s trust policy allows bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com to assume it, scoped to your account. For Web Answer, the role needs: bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer , to call Web Answer. The Gateway checks this permission on every request against the ARN that AWS owns, arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:aws:tool/web-answer.v1 . Attach the policy to the service role as an inline policy: import json import boto3 iam = boto3.client("iam") iam.put_role_policy( RoleName=" ", PolicyName="WebAnswerGuide", PolicyDocument=json.dumps({ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "InvokeWebAnswer", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebAnswer", "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:aws:tool/web-answer.v1", } ], }), ) The role controls only the Gateway’s outbound calls. Who can call your Gateway is set by its inbound authorizer. The role also doesn’t need bedrock:InvokeModel : your agent’s model runs under your agent’s own identity. items.title: METR: Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026
items.description: Executive summary From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D. If AI systems started to significantly accelerate further AI development, this could lead to a sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities . Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff. In our first section, we share our subjective conclusions about risk . We now believe that: As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025. The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks. In our second section we share some of the key empirical findings from our Full Report : Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year. We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute. Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon. We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment. Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted by Anthropic. In our third section, we describe the assessment process : The scope, setup, and timeline of this assessment. Details of the information shared with METR. Details of what information and evidence we were not able to share given Anthropic’s redactions. Finally, we describe the biggest limitations of our analysis: We could be underestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) evidence that some growth rates have further increased recently; (2) further automation of AI R&D tasks leading to a further acceleration in progress; (3) evidence that AECI growth has sometimes understated growth in real-world impact. We could be overestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) non-AI factors in Anthropic’s research progress; (2) AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks; (3) reasons why Anthropic’s early growth rate (2023–2025) was unusually low. The remainder of the report goes into detailed discussion of each of the key components. We include appendices with supplemental material. Twitter thread . Ryan Greenblatt : This report on AI R&D automation (RSI) is a big update towards ASI within 1-2 years. It says AI progress is sped up by RSI right now by around 2x. In AI 2027, this happens around March 2027. I was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026 (around 1.15x-1.3x). It seems as though there was specific privately available evidence that would have changed my mind. I haven't seen an unredacted version of this report; this is purely about the public report. Because so much of the underlying evidence was redacted from the public report, I think conclusions about things other than the observed 2x faster rate of progress on benchmarks depend significantly on trust for the authors of the report. (E.g., conclusions about whether this speed up is from RSI depend on trust.) I do trust the authors of the report a lot to be careful and rigorous and generally do a good job. (Note that I also work at METR.) Less extensive redactions would greatly reduce this need for trust. Ajeya Cotra : Our colleagues found that Anthropic’s capabilities progress has doubled, mainly due to AI. Ryan’s modeling from public info suggests the whole company’s R&D would be going 4-5x faster. Labor uplift would be higher still. This is a major update to very short timelines. I am sad that so much of the underlying evidence in this report was redacted. I think evidence transparency is very important for the world to figure this out in time. Evidence about risk should be transparent . Daniel Kokotajlo : says the METR report confirms his worry from two days ago, which was: We at AIFP are spooked by [Anthropic's S1 update]. IF (big IF) Anthropic really is imminently about to meet the RSP threshold of 2x acceleration over baseline, then it seems timelines to full RSI and superintelligence may be very short indeed. items.title: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI
items.description: A+ Content is the rich media widget on the Amazon product detail page. Through visual assets, brands communicate unique product and brand value to help customers make informed purchase decisions. Selling partners using high-quality A+ Content boost their sales by 8–20 percent compared to those without it. A wide variety of brands, from established brands with large in-house design teams to bootstrapped brands with limited resources, use A+ Content, creating inconsistency in content quality. A typical A+ Content project combines text, images, and video into a cohesive product story. Evaluating each asset in isolation misses the quality that emerges from how those assets work together. When your content spans multiple heterogeneous modules and you need a holistic quality signal rather than per-asset checks, the multi-model fusion approach described in this post can help. In this post, we examine this problem in the context of A+ Content. A+ Content provides creative freedom for selling partners to express their authentic selves on their product detail pages, without strict content specifications such as image ratio and text word count. Although this flexibility allows compelling brand storytelling, it also creates substantial variation in content composition and quality. With quality evaluation and improvement recommendations, brands can transform average content into high-quality content that is more coherent, relevant, and useful. This improved content helps customers make more informed purchasing decisions and build lasting relationships with brands, leading to improved revenue for selling partners. To achieve this goal, an evaluation system must assess the complete content experience, provide actionable recommendations beyond numeric scores, and reflect the nuances across product categories. Existing approaches struggle to meet all these requirements simultaneously, so in this post, you will see a new approach using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to understand and evaluate content holistically, and a diffusion-based generation component that produces improved visual assets from the resulting quality signals. In this post, you will learn how to: Render complete ecommerce content as a single snapshot and evaluate it holistically with a VLM. Combine VLM semantic scores with OCR readability signals in a lightweight CatBoost classifier trained on expert annotations. Use SHAP to explain quality decisions and generate actionable improvement recommendations for selling partners. Implement the end-to-end pipeline on Amazon SageMaker AI, from data ingestion and annotation through model hosting, explainability, and production monitoring. Opportunities and challenges in VLM-based evaluation A vision language model (VLM) pairs an image encoder with a large language model (LLM). The encoder, often a vision transformer (ViT) , splits an image into patches and turns them into embeddings, and a small connector maps those embeddings into the language model’s input space ( Flamingo , LLaVA ). Many VLMs reuse the image encoder from CLIP , which learned to match images with their captions. Because VLMs are trained to follow instructions, you can give one an image along with a rubric of evaluation criteria and get back a written assessment without task-specific training. When you need closer agreement with human reviewers, you can fine-tune the model on labeled examples. This makes VLMs a practical starting point for checking product images against your content guidelines at scale. Conventional computer vision models can already score individual assets, for example flagging a blurry image or a grammar error in a bullet list. Using a VLM to grade each asset separately adds little beyond that. A product detail page, however, combines images, text, and layout modules into a single story, and its quality depends on how those pieces work together. Our approach renders the full page as a single snapshot and asks the VLM to evaluate it as customers see it. Consider a blender page with a hero image, a bulleted feature list highlighting blade speed and capacity, and a lifestyle photo of the blender in a modern kitchen. Checked one by one, each asset passes: the image is sharp, the bullets are grammatical, and the photo is well lit. Viewed together, problems appear. The bullets might advertise a 64-oz pitcher while the lifestyle photo shows a single-serve model, or the lifestyle photo might sit above the hero image so customers see the kitchen before the product. Because an asset’s meaning depends on where it appears and what surrounds it, these issues only show up when the page is evaluated as a whole. The snapshot gives the VLM that complete view. Using it in production adds three requirements: scores must match expert quality standards, evaluation must be accurate and efficient at scale, and each result must explain what to fix. As shown in Figure 1, we address these considerations through a VLM-based multi-model fusion architecture designed around adaptability, performance, and explainability. The following sections describe each component. Figure 1: Block diagram of the VLM-based multi-model fusion approach, including VLM, OCR, and classifier models Adaptive VLM content evaluation with expert annotations A pretrained VLM prompted with a rubric scores content from its general knowledge, and those scores don’t always match ecommerce quality standards. Fine-tuning the VLM to close that gap would require GPU training infrastructure and, with only a few thousand labeled examples, carries a real risk of overfitting. Instead, we keep the VLM and rubric prompt fixed, use the VLM’s structured outputs as features, and train a CatBoost classifier on them to predict expert quality labels. CatBoost, a gradient-boosted decision tree library, performs well on small tabular datasets like this one. Because only the classifier is retrained, updating the system as annotations accumulate or criteria change takes a short CPU-only job

Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)
items.description: AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action? “Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. Agents can potentially take any action online that their User could, without the limits that hold humans back. They don't tire, they run around the clock, they act in parallel, and they put up with friction no person would. Much of the web, from how Sites plan capacity to how they make money, assumes those limits. Fundamentally, remotely hosted Agents are intermediaries . An intermediary is anything that sits between a User and a Site, so the Site sees it instead of the User. Agents are the newest kind of intermediary, but intermediaries have existed for a long time. Cloud browsers (hosted browsers that software controls on a User's behalf) and Proxies (services that relay a User's traffic, including VPNs) are intermediaries too. What has changed is the trajectory. Agentic traffic is growing rapidly and may eclipse traditional human browsing on the Internet in the near future. This forces a reckoning for anyone operating a Site today. Historically, a Site could simply block intermediary traffic and require Users to disable the intermediary service. That stops working when the majority of traffic is agentic. Once blocking is no longer viable, Site Operators are left with the problem that intermediaries have always created. The Site loses direct information about the User and must decide whether to trust the intermediary without it. This post covers Agents hosted somewhere other than the User's device. Local agents (e.g. OpenClaw) or Agents running in the User's own browser, on their own device, are out of scope of the primary topic addressed by this post (see below, "On open source and local Agents"). This post rests on one principle: The Intermediation Principle : The business relationship between Users and Sites, and each participant’s security responsibilities, must be upheld regardless of intermediation. A Site needs new tools to recognize, serve, and hold accountable a User acting through an Agent just as it could if that User had visited directly. The Agent, and the Operator behind it, must be recognizable and accountable too, because an Agent can do what no User could. Agents are able to scale human access almost without limit, so they create new risks, even for behavior that was previously benign. The intermediary problem Meet Ezra. Ezra works as a personal assistant for people in her city. Her best client is Amy, a local CEO, but she also works for Bob, Charlie, and Debra. She runs their errands: groceries, appointments, paperwork, and flights. Ezra blends into the crowd. The corner grocer used to know Amy. He knew what she bought and set aside what he thought she'd like. Now only Ezra comes in, carrying orders for four people, and the grocer can't tell whose preferences are whose. He doesn't want to turn Ezra away, because she brings him a lot of business. Then Bob asks Ezra to buy him an iPhone. A week later he calls the store, says he never authorized the charge, and keeps the phone. To win the dispute, the store has to prove Bob asked for it. But the only person the store ever saw was Ezra. Then Charlie gives Ezra a list of passwords: "I forgot mine, but it's one of these." Ezra patiently tries each one at Charlie's bank. The bank can see an attack happening, but the only person it can ban is Ezra. Banning Ezra also bans Amy, Bob, and Debra. None of these business owners has a problem with Ezra herself. Their problem is that they can only see Ezra, not the person she's acting for. Swap Ezra for an AI Agent and the businesses for websites, and you have the web today. A website owner wants sufficient visibility both to prevent bad behavior and to effectively monetize or get value from their Site. But as with Ezra, much of that visibility goes away with AI Agents. Below is a list of actions that a website owner might want to address that were previously solved, but are made more challenging by allowing Agents. In nearly every challenge above, the Site bears the primary cost . That outcome follows from how trust works when an intermediary is involved. Our vision Our aim is an Internet where all Users have equal or greater access to websites than they had before. Before Agents, a Site was typically able to mitigate these risks with a collection of techniques, including fingerprinting the User’s device, session, and history. Users could still browse using private browsing mode, and we believe Agents should be able to do that as well. But they probably won’t be able to log in to a bank without additional verification. None of this requires an Agent to act like a human or a human to be present for every action. items.title: The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models
items.description: Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it. “We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers. Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is YouTube , where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents. “I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.” Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it. “Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.” That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents. “I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. And that is Nemotron.” https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ChrisAlexiuk_captions_9MB.mp4 It’s this matter-of-fact directness and affable approachability that makes Alexiuk’s teaching style so appealing. On the social media platform X, he goes by the handle “llm_wizard.” His avatar: a laughing cartoon caricature sporting a slouchy sorcerer’s hat and brandishing a magic wand. It’s no surprise, then, that Alexiuk likens Nemotron to a magical library — its users fellow wizards in search of knowledge that can move mountains. “You’re a wizard in search of prepared spells, and Nemotron has a spell for everything,” he said. “Just choose the one you need.” In non-wizard terms? “There’s a category of model that’s going to be close to the kind of work you want to accomplish,” Alexiuk said, explaining that Nemotron supports that whole ecosystem of AI users: from individual developers using a model like Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for repetitive, high-frequency execution work to a company deploying Nemotron Ultra for long-running autonomous agents, deep research and enterprise tasks. NVIDIAN Chris Alexiuk (left) engages with developers during the Build-a-Claw event at GTC Berlin. “I think that openness helps more people understand AI and hopefully leads to more people doing really ingenious things with these tools at the limit,” Alexiuk said. “If a tool is amplifying skill, it’s amplifying human expression.” From Birding to Model-Building Alexiuk first became fascinated with machine learning in a computational physics class at Trent University in Ontario, Canada. “After that, I learned about TensorFlow and that you could build image classifiers that ran on your GPU,” he recalled. As an initial one-off project, Alexiuk built a classifier that would alert him whenever his friend’s distinctive pet bird, a Yellow-Faced Gray Budgerigar, appeared in frame on his webcam during shared video game sessions. “Because we were playing video games, I wasn’t focused on my friend’s webcam, but I didn’t want to miss seeing the bird when it appeared,” Alexiuk said. “And then my whole life changed, because in that instance I realized it’s crazy what you could do with technology.” Since then, he’s been embedding himself in the open source AI community. “To imagine within the span of a few years going from freaking out because I could know my friend’s bird was in the camera frame to being able to make any website in a matter of minutes with a model that’s running on my laptop — I cannot wait to see what’s next,” Alexiuk said. “It’s never been more accessible to get into and learn about AI.” And if another LLM wizard arises to challenge him for the title of No. 1 Nemotron Fan? “It would be the greatest day of my life to be surpassed by an even bigger fan of Nemotron, who had heard about Nemotron through the work I was doing,” Alexiuk said. “That would be a capstone to my career that I can only dream of.” Hear more from Alexiuk by following the NVIDIA Nemotron Labs Livestreams series on YouTube.

items.title: AI Text Watermarking May Not Be Able to Meet the EU’s New Rules
items.description: The European Union now requires AI-generated text to be watermarked so that it can be identified as such. But tests on OpenAI’s new textGrain watermark, released in October and developed to comply with the new EU law , show that these watermarks often do not survive additional editing of the text or when it’s under 150 words. With no clear legal benchmark for how well watermarks should work, it’s uncertain whether textGrain will meet Europe’s transparency rules, which could cost the company significantly and make it difficult to detect AI-generated text as models grow more sophisticated. AI models calculate the probabilities of different possible next tokens (the next word or word fragment it generates) based on the text already written, then select one and repeat that process until the response is complete. After the prompt “today the weather is…,” for example, says Xiang Li , co-author of the textGrain technical report and a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Pennsylvania, the model might weigh “warm” or “cool” as possible next words. A watermark uses a secret key to generate pseudorandom values: numbers produced by a mathematical process, which influence which token the model suggests. This creates a statistical pattern in the text that a detector with the same secret key can look for, Li says. What makes textGrain different from other watermarks is that it uses entropy, a measure of how unpredictable a model’s word choices are, as a resource that can be budgeted when embedding a watermark. Developers specify how much entropy or unpredictability they want to allow, and textGrain adjusts to that target. This gives developers more control over the balance between embedding a detectable signal and preserving variation in the model’s output, Li says. “We can think of entropy as a resource, a kind of money. […] In our approach, we can accurately determine how much of that resource we want to consume.” Limits of AI Watermark Detection The watermark is invisible to readers. But a positive result does not show how much a person contributed to a passage, and a negative result does not prove that a text was human-written. OpenAI’s false-positive rate is 1 percent, meaning the detector is designed to wrongly flag about one in 100 unwatermarked passages. In tests on psychology questions from the ELI5 database , which gathers questions and answers from the /r/explainlikeimfive subreddit, the model detected watermarks in about 80 percent of 200-token text ( approximately 150 words ) compared to 95 percent of 400-token text (approximately 300 words). Li says this is a “basic limitation” of text watermarking technologies and would be complicated to solve. Short passages may not contain enough watermark evidence for reliable detection, even with additional computation, he adds, while longer passages generally provide more. Editing also weakens the signal. In an evaluation of 400-token passages, replacing just 10 percent of words with synonyms reduced detection from 92 percent to 66 percent; replacing up to 25 percent cut the detection rate to 17 percent, according to OpenAI. Because the watermark depends on preceding tokens, changing one word can disrupt the signal at several positions, Li says. OpenAI says watermarking alone is not enough to determine whether content is AI-generated. TextGrain will “complement” other provenance tools, such as content credentials in the metadata and SynthID watermarks developed by Google DeepMind for images and audio outputs. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. EU AI Act Transparency Obligations The transparency obligations in Article 50 of the EU AI Act went into effect on 2 August. The law requires providers of systems generating synthetic audio, images, video, or text to mark outputs in a machine-readable format so they can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated. Technical solutions must be “effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as this is technically feasible,” according to the law. The EU’s Code of Practice offers a voluntary way for providers to show how they will be compliant. This code does not require watermarks on outputs shorter than 200 tokens. Thomas Souverain , a postdoctoral fellow on AI Ethics at the Institute of Advanced Education in Paris, says the legislation is open to interpretation. Souverain says that the early methodology behind textGrain seems reliable and could work better than its competitors at identifying AI-generated text. OpenAI says textGrain matched or outperformed Google’s SynthID Text in its own tests, but those results have not been independently verified. Until independent researchers can test it, and while the AI Act’s criteria still lack measurable thresholds, it is too early to say whether textGrain meets legal requirements. “We only have a technical study … there hasn’t been a peer-reviewed academic article, and we don’t [yet] have access to a precise protocol [for textGrain],” Souverain says. OpenAI is working with a limited group of researchers that includes John Thickstun , an assistant professor of computer science at Cornell University, and researchers at the Kempelen Institute of Intelligent Technologies in Bratislava, Slovakia. Thickstun and Dominik Macko , a senior researcher at KInIT, says they had only just gained access and had not yet begun evaluating the system. Macko says his team plans to test textGrain’s “robustness” across different subject areas, languages, and text lengths. If textGrain is eventually found to not meet the EU’s requirements, Souverain says OpenAI could face a fine of up to 7 percent of its annual income. Souverain also calls on OpenAI to make textGrain open-source so that researchers not on their team can “identify all the faults, paraphrases and possible translation faults” of the model by trying to break it. “I see the corporate interest, if there is a big flaw detected, a big weakness, [that] it is detected in the background,” he said. “Bu

items.title: Agility Robotics' Nasdaq debut invites scrutiny of humanoid robot market
items.description: Humanoid robots remain unproven at scale and have not yet achieved widespread commercialization, compared with industrial robots that have decades of proven track records in warehouses and factories. That frank acknowledgment is among the risks outlined in a securities filing by Agility Robotics—the first dedicated developer of humanoid robots to become a publicly traded company in the United States. The robotics company, headquartered in Salem, Oregon, previously became the first to achieve full-time commercial deployment of humanoid robots at a customer warehouse in 2024. Now, Agility’s public listing on the Nasdaq stock exchange as of November 5 has come with financial disclosures detailing how the company plans to build a business around renting out or selling humanoid robots to perform manual labor. “When we are doing robots as a service, it is much lower risk for customers to use it because they are getting a return on investment on day one,” Jonathan Hurst , co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics, told Ars. "Because they're paying a rate that is comparable to the human labor rate, and that makes the economics pretty straightforward.” Read full article Comments

items.title: Entity-Aware Evaluation of OCR Systems for Historical Document Transcription
items.description: arXiv:2610.33004v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is essential for digitizing historical archives, yet standard evaluation metrics such as Character Error Rate (CER) do not necessarily reflect whether meaningful information, such as names, dates, and identifiers, is preserved. In this work, we investigate entitylevel analysis of OCR errors as a complementary perspective for evaluating OCR quality in historical documents. Using a publicly available benchmark of 175 documents from the Berrutti Archive, augmented with 5,209 manually annotated entity mentions that will be released upon acceptance, we compare sequence-recognition OCR systems, OCR-specialized vision-language models, and general-purpose vision-language models. Beyond global transcription accuracy, we analyze entity preservation and recoverability under varying character-level edit tolerances. Our experiments show that OCR rankings depend on the evaluation criterion: while Qwen 3.6 achieves the highest entity coverage across all tested tolerances, several systems with lower exact-match coverage recover substantially when small errors are tolerated, suggesting that many of their errors correspond to localized character-level deviations rather than fundamentally incorrect entity transcriptions. Conversely, some systems remain unable to recover many entities even under relaxed matching. These findings show that OCR quality cannot be fully characterized by aggregate transcription metrics alone and highlight the importance of evaluating how OCR errors affect the preservation and recoverability of meaningful information.

items.title: Labadain-MedQA: A Tetun Medical QA Dataset for Fine-Tuning and Evaluating Large Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.00935v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have created opportunities for cross-lingual transfer of medical knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages to support access to healthcare information. However, medical question-answering (QA) datasets for fine-tuning and evaluating LLMs remain scarce for Tetun. To address this gap, we translated MedAlpaca's Medical Flashcards and WikiDoc Patient Information collections into Tetun using Gemini 2.5 Flash, producing 39,077 medical QA pairs. Translation quality was assessed on 50 randomly sampled QA pairs (100 documents) using automatic metrics against human reference translations and evaluations by two native Tetun-speaking healthcare professionals, focusing on medical accuracy and Tetun fluency. Human translations achieved higher mean ratings than LLM-generated translations for both criteria (4.43/5 vs. 4.02/5), with statistically significant differences (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.001). To assess downstream utility, we fine-tuned Gemma and Llama variants on the translated MedAlpaca dataset using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and evaluated them on 325 Tetun-translated United States Medical Licensing Examination multiple-choice questions. Gemma 4 12B fine-tuned using QLoRA achieved relative improvements in mean accuracy of 10.79% with 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) inference and 10.42% after merging the LoRA adapters into the BF16 base model, compared with the corresponding base models. These results highlight the viability of automatic dataset translation for Tetun medical QA and the effectiveness of PEFT in enhancing model performance. The datasets, models, and evaluation resources are accessible at https://github.com/labadain/labadain-medqa to support reproducible research on Tetun medical QA and facilitate machine translation, cross lingual, and multilingual research.

items.title: The Scope Grammar of Natural-Language Rules: Counting and Enumerating Readings modulo Logical Equivalence
items.description: arXiv:2611.01825v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A rule written for people fixes its atomic conditions and connectives but leaves open how the connectives are bracketed, and each bracketing is a different logical reading that an autoformalizer must resolve or expose. We study the scope grammar, a deliberately ambiguous context-free grammar whose derivation trees are the readings of a connective skeleton and whose quotient by logical equivalence is what matters downstream. A skeleton with $k$ binary connectives has $C_k$ derivation trees, the $k$-th Catalan number, but far fewer logically distinct readings. For the positive, repetition-free fragment we make the gap exact: through the uniqueness of the read-once normal form we characterize the realizable normal forms by lowest common ancestors and count them with a two-label recurrence over the operator word, verified against exhaustive enumeration up to eleven atoms. The count is invariant under reversal and $\wedge/\vee$ duality; a skeleton is ambiguous if and only if it uses both $\wedge$ and $\vee$, a one-pass test; and the number of classes is at least $2^{\lfloor n/3\rfloor}$. Up to fifteen atoms the alternating pattern is the worst case; its count has a cubic generating function, is the 3-Schr\"oder sequence (OEIS A137842), and grows with base $\varphi^{5/2}\approx3.330$, below the Catalan base 4. We reduce maximality to an inequality on increments, verified to sixteen atoms, and explain why local exchange arguments cannot prove it. We also treat negation, exceptions, and background axioms, where normal-form uniqueness still decides equivalence but counting is open.

items.title: EntropyCache: Decoded Token Entropy Guided KV Caching for Diffusion Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2603.18489v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) rely on bidirectional attention, which prevents lossless KV caching and requires a full forward pass at every denoising step. Existing approximate KV caching methods reduce this cost by selectively updating cached states, but their decision overhead scales with context length or model depth. We propose EntropyCache, a training-free KV caching method that uses the maximum entropy of newly decoded token distributions as a constant-cost signal for deciding when to recompute. Our design is grounded in two empirical observations: (1) decoded token entropy correlates with KV cache drift, providing a cheap proxy for cache staleness, and (2) feature volatility of decoded tokens persists for multiple steps after unmasking, motivating recomputation of the $k$ most recently decoded tokens. The skip-or-recompute decision requires only $O(V)$ computation per step, independent of context length and model scale. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show that EntropyCache achieves $15.2\times$-$26.4\times$ speedup on standard benchmarks and $22.4\times$-$24.1\times$ on chain-of-thought benchmarks, with competitive accuracy and decision overhead accounting for only $0.5\%$ of inference time. Code is available at https://github.com/mscheong01/EntropyCache.

items.title: Digital sovereignty in professional translation workflows: a case study of migrating from Windows to Linux
items.description: arXiv:2610.41561v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study examines digital sovereignty in professional translation through a screening of computer-assisted translation tools and translation management systems, and a case study of migrating a translator's workstation from Windows to Linux. The framework combines three principles - Control, Continuity and Exit - with three practical requirements: native Linux operation, independence from mandatory external services, and independent access to essential data and resources. Drawing on documentary evidence and the limited number of responses received from providers, the ecosystem screening distinguishes Linux accessibility from operational independence: browser-based platforms may remain dependent on provider-controlled infrastructure. The migration case demonstrates the feasibility of reconstructing one professional workflow around a locally operable Linux core, using LoopCAT, LibreOffice and locally run TranslateGemma, alongside tools for optical character recognition, communication, credential management and backup. Selected cloud services remained available where needed. The findings suggest that digital sovereignty depends on how workflow dependencies are organized, rather than on individual applications or operating systems. It does not require technological isolation, but meaningful control over essential components, continuity of work and practical exit options. The framework is tailored to the case examined here and may require adaptation to other professional workflows.

items.title: Where Is the "Self" of a Large Language Model? -- From Self-Index to Self-Reference
items.description: arXiv:2610.16717v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Whether a large language model has a self is usually argued without a way to measure it. We measure a functional self with two levels familiar from biology: a self-index, which marks material as the model's own, as animals tag self-generated signals with a corollary discharge, and self-reference, the ability to recognize what is one's own, as in mirror self-recognition. Our main finding is that language models mark their own messages in their internal representations and that recognizing these messages depends on this mark: no model we tested recognizes its own messages without it, and in the three models we edited, changing the mark removes or creates the recognition. We place the same text in an Assistant, a User, or a System message of the model's own chat template. In Qwen3.8-27B, the representation separates the model's own message from both external sources at every one of its 64 layers and in every held-out text. Asked who wrote a message, the model answers "you" with probability 0.77 for its own messages and at most 0.07 for the others. At each layer, we find eight directions along which the model's own message differs most from the same text as a User message. Giving the model's own message the User values along these directions lowers the rate of "you" to at most 0.05. Giving a User message the model's own values makes the model claim it, closing 41-67% of the gap between the two messages. Edits along eight random directions do neither. This holds in Qwen3.8-27B without and with thinking, gpt-oss-20b, and gpt-oss-120b. Across twenty-five open-weight models from fourteen developers, the two levels are nested: no model recognizes its own messages without a self-index, a pattern that would arise by chance with probability 0.004 if the levels were unrelated. These results support the account that self-reference is a readout of a self-index.

items.title: TensorSSM: Memorizing Spatial Position in Dynamic State Space for Tensor Core Generation
items.description: arXiv:2610.40871v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-dimensional tensors are ubiquitous in real-world applications but lead to massive storage overhead. Functional tensor decomposition addresses this by employing neural networks to map element coordinates to tensor cores, significantly reducing the parameters for data compression. However, existing functional methods typically flatten high-order tensors into 1D sequences. This folding operation causes highly overlapping local coordinate sequences and struggles to capture complex cross-mode spatial dependencies, severely limiting their expressiveness on diverse datasets. To tackle these challenges, we propose TensorSSM, a novel Implicit Neural Representation (INR) for functional decomposition method that memorizes spatial positions within a dynamic State Space Model (SSM). Specifically, TensorSSM first decomposes mode-wise coordinates into sequences spit by K-ary rule, encoding spatial tokens from coarse to fine, which effectively captures spatial variations. Furthermore, we extend the SSM's state space to explicitly map cross-mode spatial dependencies, allowing inter-mode interactions to enhance the updates of each mode. By integrating cross-mode information from previous hidden states into the current state transitions, TensorSSM effectively expands tensor representation along two dimensions: the sequence dimension for coarse-to-fine spatial tokens, and the state dimension for cross-mode memorization. This design effectively integrates spatial information into the state space and the tensor core, substantially advancing the state adaptability and enhancing the expressiveness of the data compression. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TensorSSM achieves significantly high reconstruction accuracy and storage efficiency, exhibiting robust expressiveness across diverse tensor datasets without relying on strict spatial assumptions.

items.title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations
items.description: arXiv:2610.37381v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.

items.title: When Disclosure Is Compulsory: Evaluating Ride-Hailing Rebalancing Policies with Self-Interested LLM Driver Agents
items.description: arXiv:2610.41132v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The EU Platform Work Directive, to be transposed by December 2026, requires ride-hailing platforms to state in plain language the main parameters of their automated decisions and how a worker's behaviour affects them. Such rules are exactly what a large language model (LLM) can read, so drivers will be able to let one decide for them. We compare two main families of rebalancing policy once their rules are public: a reactive policy (R) that sends idle drivers to cover requests just lost, and an anticipatory policy (A) that plans moves on a demand forecast. Each driver is an LLM agent maximizing its own net income, given no rules (N) or the rules at the directive's level of detail (L). We test two LLMs, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Jev, which understand the rules equally well, in a three-zone model and in Manhattan. With the rules disclosed, drivers follow the platform more closely: in Manhattan, the share of relocation offers they decline falls from about four in five to one in four under both policies. Yet the effects differ by policy. For the platform, disclosure costs R 3.7% of its profit in Manhattan, as R now pays for moves drivers used to make for free, while A's profit is unchanged; the two policies, which tie on profit under full compliance, end 6.1% apart. For drivers, disclosure raises income in the small model under both policies and LLMs; for users, it raises the service rate there by 10 to 18 percentage points. In Manhattan, self-interested drivers also make A a win-win-win against full compliance, raising driver income, platform profit and service rate by 10 to 12% each. Rebalancing policies that perform equally well under full compliance can thus show opposite results under mandatory disclosure. The study offers a framework to evaluate such policies under the new requirement and is, to our knowledge, the first to do so with LLM agents.

items.title: Tactus: Tactile & Pose Sensing Glove for Natural Dexterity Data Collection
items.description: arXiv:2610.39076v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Collecting naturalistic human manipulation demonstrations with accurate contact force and hand pose is essential for robot dexterous manipulation policy and foundational world model learning - yet no existing wearable platform provides both calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation behavior. We present Tactus, a textile-integrated sensing glove that co-optimizes three design pillars: (1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5 mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies, and (3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable. Tactus includes a documented calibration pipeline for cross-glove consistency and per-session calibration for subject-dependent correction.
