items.title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
items.description: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail. Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself. Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether. The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium. That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana. The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects. Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it. A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere. It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red. This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices. Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

items.title: Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
items.description: Some of the questions you ask when evaluating an agent are narrow and repeatable. Did this response stay on policy? Is this tool call safe to approve? Does this answer match the retrieved context? Decision models answer exactly that kind of question. They take a structured state and a fixed set of allowed answers and return a calibrated probability over them, rather than free-form text whose confidence drifts from run to run. That makes them a strong fit for the scoring step in an agent evaluation, where you want a label and a number you can threshold and trust. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scores an agent through its entire lifecycle, on demand during development, in batch jobs against stored sessions, and online against production traffic. Alongside 15 built-in evaluators, AgentCore Evaluations supports custom evaluators that you define as either an LLM-as-a-judge or a code-based evaluator. Custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluators apply your instructions and rating scale with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Code-based evaluators run your own logic in an AWS Lambda function, and that logic can call your choice of external system, model, or API, including a decision model. Decision models suit questions with a fixed set of answers that an informed person could decide at a glance, such as whether the agent refused a request or whether a response stayed on topic. After you validate a question on your own traffic, a decision model can be sufficient for that decision or score, and you can extend the same approach to specific harmfulness or stereotyping categories in your policy. Because both backends can answer several questions about the same state in a single request, you can use them as a screening layer rather than a replacement, running a pass or fail signal across your metrics to select the turns that warrant deeper assessment by the built-in evaluators, whose explanations help you investigate what went wrong. This post shows how to connect two decision model backends to AgentCore Evaluations through code-based evaluators. The first is Jev , a hosted decision model from TypeSafe. The second is Strands Decider 2B , an open-source decision model you run yourself. By the end of this post, you will know how to convert the AgentCore evaluator input into a decision model request, and the model’s probabilities back into an AgentCore evaluation result. First, though, when should you reach for a custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluator, and when does a decision model fit better? The next section breaks down what a decision model is and the trade-offs involved. Decision models A decision model is a small, specialized model trained to select from a fixed set of options and return calibrated confidence scores rather than generating free-form text. A general-purpose large language model (LLM) evaluator produces a score with a rationale. A decision model instead produces a probability distribution over predefined answers. That gives you a direct confidence measure you can threshold, aggregate, and act on programmatically. This makes decision models well-suited for evaluation tasks where the judgment can be stated as a choice among a fixed set of options: “Is this response grounded?” or “Did the agent complete the user’s goal?” Decision models are most useful when you want a well-calibrated confidence score alongside the label, not just a binary judgment. They are also appropriate when you want to enforce a specific rubric consistently without relying on a general-purpose LLM to interpret it. Jev, the hosted decision model from TypeSafe, and Strands Decider , an open-source, 2-billion-parameter decision model from the Strands Agents team, both support three types of questions. A noul question poses a yes/no question and returns a probability between 0 (no) and 1 (yes). A choice question asks which of up to 255 options applies, returning the most probable option along with the full distribution and a confidence. A score question asks which of 2 to 10 ordered levels applies, returning a probability-weighted score, the distribution over levels, and a confidence. Many evaluation rubrics fit one of these types. “Is every fact in this response supported by the tool results?” is a yes/no question, and “How helpful was this response, on a four-level rubric?” is a score. Decision models versus LLM-as-a-judge The built-in evaluators in AgentCore today use a general-purpose LLM to assess the agent response against a rubric and explain its judgment. This is valuable when the evaluation requires connecting evidence, identifying missing information, or working through a response in depth in tasks where the explanation is as useful as the score. Decision models are not a replacement for LLM evaluators. They’re an addition that the code-based evaluator framework makes possible. Use them for narrow, well-defined checks alongside the built-in evaluators’ broader assessment. Solution overview To show how these evaluator types work together, this post builds an end-to-end example of an HR Assistant agent evaluated by deterministic code-based checks, built-in LLM-as-a-judge evaluators, and decision-model evaluators backed by Jev or Strands Decider 2B. The agent is built with Strands Agents and deployed to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It answers employee questions using five tools that return fixed mock data such as paid time off (PTO) balances, PTO requests, HR policies, benefits, and pay stubs. We use fixed data in this code sample to make it straightforward to verify evaluator behavior from LLM-as-a-judge and decision models. When you additionally have ground truth, you can confirm whether each evaluator catches the right failures. This code sample helps you set up the framework for testing decision models compared to LLM-as-a-judge for your own use cases. items.title: Positive and Negative AI Futures
items.description: I'm continuing to share some notes I created for myself to use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I really like using Ilya: the AI scientist shaping the world as a way of engaging students at the start of a course. The video primarily focuses on the way that AI could go wrong, however, it also starts with “Now, AI is a great thing…”, so it naturally leads to a discussion of positive and negative futures. Positive Futures: One obvious resource on positive futures Foresight Institute’s Existential Hope website. I’ve browsed their content in the past, some of it is kind of interesting, but honestly, I found view it as mostly pretty mid. They also run a fellowship which has an existential hope stream: They recently released The AI future nobody is showing you , which resulted in a wide range of reactions on Twitter. I think this is worth commenting on as it illustrates the challenges with attempting to produce a positive vision. Honestly, I’ve become quite pessimistic here: the gap between what different groups in society want may simply be too wide for it to be possible to find a positive vision that unites society: Steven Pinker was positive: “A more plausible vision, in my view, than either Utopia or doom.” Nikola Jurkovic was in the middle: “I admire the effort… but sadly this story falls into the common narrative trap of just assuming that AGI won’t actually be deployed widely.” @HellenicVibes hated it: “Wow how exciting to have a thousand years under the boot of ‘community leaders,’ ‘impacted minorities,’ and ‘AI auditors!’ I would literally rather be turned into paperclips.” Would it matter if there doesn’t exist a unifying positive vision? What’s wrong with different people having different visions of a positive future? Well, I wouldn’t say anything is wrong with people having different visions per se, but I suspect it makes navigating the path forward much harder, even if everyone broadly agrees that certain outcomes would be bad. Whilst Dario wrote Machines of Loving Grace that argued most people were under-estimating the update he has also argued that the public’s current negative perception of AI is unlikely to shift in response to messaging (“a glitzy marketing campaign”). He argues that it is fundamentally a matter of trust with the causes going back decades. What matters is not talking about curing cancer, but “actually curing cancer” or other diseases. Forethought has a series on Better Futures which argues that Flourishing is currently underrated relative to surviving on the basis of scale and neglectedness. I think the series should actually be called “Best Futures” as that’s his true focus, largely as a result of his (mostly) risk-neutral stance. There is also a course , though “Better Futures work” is something of a misnomer as that implies more distinctness from standard x-risk/catastrophic risk work than this is given that the Better Futures perspective only makes most such work more important on the margin. Negative Futures: It’s worth remembering that the Ilya video started with him saying, “Now, AI is a great thing…” Of course, by the time you get to the end of the video and you’ve heard all the ways this can go wrong, it’s very easy to forget that he said that and reduce him to a “doomer” when he actually believes that AI can be built safely . Dario has complained about this phenomenon too. In response to criticism that he should be “more of a positive advocate for his own industry”, Dario has claimed that his messaging has been “equally balanced between risks and benefits” and that people may be misunderstanding his views because negative clips are disproportionately likely to go viral. In There’s No Rule That Says We Make it , Rob Miles claims that people often have an implicit belief that humanity will “rise to the occasion” even if they wouldn’t actually endorse that statement. He suggests that this may derive from fiction, where we face challenges, but we almost always overcome then. He dismisses this fictional “evidence” as not real evidence. Whilst Rob is talking about existential risk, you could apply his argument more broadly to less severe risks as well. Intermediate Futures: Utopia or dystopia certainly aren’t the only two possibilities. There’s also the chance of an intermediate path and I wanted to mention it here for balance since most of the material in the course will stand in opposition to this perspective. One particularly prominent perspective in this vein is AI as a Normal Technology : “Transformative economic and societal impacts will be slow (on the timescale of decades)… We do not think that viewing AI as a humanlike intelligence is currently accurate or useful for understanding its societal impacts, nor is it likely to be in our vision of the (foreseeable) future (their timescale here is vague, but they concede that their view “has failed and/or is no longer useful” if “strong AI” is “developed and deployed in the next decade”).” ( summary , guide , critique by AI Futures Project , common ground , viral music video critique “Thus Spoke Compute” ). Their project has three elements: A description of current AI A prediction about the foreseeable future A prescription about how we should respond (I have an instinctual reaction that using a single catchy phrase “AI as a Normal Technology” as a framework for answering three separate questions feels “too neat”. I acknowledge that simplicity is a virtue of an analytical framework andI admit this is a shallow objection, but nonetheless I do see this as a yellow flag). Additional detail: They have a three stage model of technological progress: invention, innovation and diffusion. They argue things will move slowly as further invention often requires additional learnings or data which can only come from iteratively diffusing/deploying the technology. items.title: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters
items.description: How should security leaders preserve human oversight as AI agents take on more work? Permissions establish which actions agents can take, but a permitted action can still warrant a person’s judgment. Requiring approval for every step might seem like the safest approach, yet multi-step tasks can produce repeated prompts , even for routine actions. Research on security warnings shows that attention and adherence can decline with repetition. The challenge isn’t to require more approvals, but to preserve attention for decisions that need human review. Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls. It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review. It does this without granting additional permissions or removing required human approvals. Security leaders retain control over which actions must always go to a person, while Smart Approvals is designed to reduce unnecessary interruptions in routine work. Figure 1: Policy determines eligibility. Smart Approvals approves eligible actions or returns them to the user for review. Policy denials remain blocked Policy sets the boundary Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review. Denied actions remain denied, and mandatory human approvals still apply. With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval. Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions. Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals. It’s on by default, but profiles with deny-by-default enabled must explicitly allow it. Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs. When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account-level setting can turn it back on for them. How eligible actions are reviewed Smart Approvals uses a separate model, the classifier, to evaluate eligible actions against the user’s request and a bounded view of the conversation. It considers what the action does, where data goes, and who it affects. It can consult the user’s knowledge graph, which contains people and working relationships drawn from connected sources. This helps it understand how recipients relate to the user, such as whether a recipient is in the user’s reporting chain. This lookup stays within your Quick account. Quick doesn’t use the content the classifier reviews, including knowledge graph data, to train models or improve the service. An action can match the request and still warrant human review. Examples include sending content outside the organization or to senior leaders in the user’s reporting chain, changing access, deleting records, or initiating payments. This list isn’t complete, and the classifier also weighs the surrounding context. Reviewing actions against the user’s request adds a check against indirect prompt injection, where instructions in retrieved content attempt to redirect the agent. Quick instructs both the agent and classifier to treat that content as information, not instructions. Model review can still make mistakes, so actions that must always receive human approval, including those that move sensitive data, should require it through connector action permissions. The classifier provides judgment. The permission service enforces authority. Each automatic approval is single-use, applies only to the exact action and parameters reviewed, and grants no ongoing permission. Quick labels automatic approvals in the conversation. Actions the classifier doesn’t approve return to the user, as do timeouts and other review failures, which never grant automatic approval. These enforcement boundaries limit what an approval authorizes. They don’t establish that the classifier’s judgment was correct. When an action goes beyond the request An account manager asks Quick to prepare a quarterly business review brief for AnyCompany using her team’s account notes and last quarter’s email. She then asks Quick to send it to two colleagues she names. Assuming the send is eligible for automated review, Smart Approvals evaluates the proposed action against her request and the available conversation context. Now suppose an account note says the brief should also go to an all-sales distribution list of about 2,000 people. That would change the audience beyond the recipients she specified, so Smart Approvals is designed to return the proposed send to her for review, where she can decline it. An approval to send to the original recipients can’t be reused for the wider audience. Audit evidence and investigation The Quick permission service records permission updates associated with Smart Approvals in AWS CloudTrail in your account. Each event identifies the user, connector, action, and time, and marks the request as associated with Smart Approvals. That marker doesn’t establish that the permission service accepted the grant or that the action ran. Quick also records permission-check verdicts, including denials from connector action permissions, and changes to a user’s Smart Approvals setting. Investigators can correlate these events by user and time with other Quick activity in CloudTrail and logs delivered through Amazon CloudWatch Logs . Chat logs capture the user’s request, system response, and conversation context. Agent metadata logs record changes to agents. Records from the destination system, such as a sent email or updated ticket, confirm whether the action completed. Together, these sources help reconstruct what happened without treating approval as proof of execution. CloudTrail Event history retains events for 90 days,

items.title: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code
items.description: When production AI agents handle tasks such as data analysis and report generation, context management can become a major bottleneck. A 200K-token window sounds generous until a real-world task burns through most of it in minutes. Data analysis and report generation leave the agent failing mid-execution, losing accuracy, or driving up costs. A body of published guidance already addresses this, but the individual techniques are easier to read about than to apply. Applied together, they make a measurable difference: in the reference implementation this post walks through, a single write-and-execute tool cuts the tokens each script adds to context by about 95 percent, and loading skills on demand shrinks the system prompt by about 97 percent. This series organizes that guidance into practices you can apply directly. Anthropic’s engineering posts, together with features built into the Strands Agents SDK, converge on four layers of context engineering: isolate context at the architecture level, control it through prompts, externalize it to the filesystem, and verify it with independent agents and safeguards. In this post (Part 2), you will learn how each layer works and what it looks like in working code. We applied these techniques in Deep Insight , an open source multi-agent data analysis solution built on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which serves as the reference implementation throughout. Post series Part 1: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them. Part 2: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code. Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production. (Coming soon!) The first post defined five core challenges that production multi-agent systems must solve. It introduced how Strands Agents SDK , Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore , and AWS Fargate each address different layers of the problem, with code examples. This second post takes the four layers of context engineering practice that sit on top of that architecture and shows each one implemented. The third post guides you through deploying and operating agents in a secure private network on Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), covering everything needed for real-world operations. What is context engineering? Context engineering is the discipline of optimizing the information in a large language model (LLM)’s limited context window so agents perform at their best. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5, available on Amazon Bedrock, offers a 200K context window, but complex production tasks quickly exceed it. For example, a seemingly straightforward request like “ Analyze sales data and create a DOCX report ” runs through several stages: data loading and exploration (5 min), category-based sales analysis (3 min), generating five charts for time-series analysis (10 min), statistical validation (3 min), and final report generation (5 min). Together they consume over 150K tokens across 15 minutes. Processing such tasks in a single context causes problems: the window overflows mid-task, stale context degrades performance, and errors require re-running the whole pipeline. As context grows, attention to important information drops, and inefficiency raises cost under per-token pricing. “As the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model’s ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases (Context rot).” — Anthropic, “ Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents ” (2025.09) Context engineering solves exactly these problems, and it is not only a collection of techniques. Spanning architecture design, prompt writing, tool implementation, and verification, it’s a layered discipline where each layer compensates for what the previous ones miss. This post details the four-layer approach you can apply to manage context efficiently. How to handle tasks that exceed the context window Anthropic has published several techniques for handling long-horizon tasks. Deep Insight groups these techniques into four layers, with each layer addressing the limitations of the others. The following table sets out the four layers. Layer Practice Core Principle Limitations Layer 1: Architecture Isolating Context Through Multi-Agent Architecture Each agent operates in an independent context When isolation alone is not enough Layer 2: Prompt Output Control and Behavioral Rules Limiting context intake through prompts When prompts alone are not enough Layer 3: Tools File-based Context Externalization Keeping heavy content in files outside the context When issues still arise Layer 4: Verification Agents and Safeguards Independent Verification and Safeguards Catching errors and preventing context overflow Final line of defense The sections that follow take each layer in order, stating what the layer prescribes, why the preceding layers alone are insufficient, and how the practice is implemented in Deep Insight. 1. Isolating context through multi-agent architecture Give each specialized agent its own context window and pass only compressed results to the orchestrator. Deep Insight does this with a hierarchy of Coordinator, Planner, Plan Reviewer, Supervisor, and Tool Agents (Coder, Validator, Reporter, Tracker, Auditor). With a single agent, all information, from user requests through data exploration, analysis, chart generation, validation, and reporting, accumulates in one context and easily exceeds the window. Giving each agent its own context keeps even the Coder, which uses the most, under 25K tokens total. Each agent receives only what it needs and signals others with a completion notice and brief summary. The key to isolation is minimizing shared information. Deep Insight uses a Python dictionary, shared_state , that stores only four things: messages : The previous agent’s final message (not the full conversation history). clues : Compressed summaries collected from each agent. full_p

items.title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences
items.description: This post is co-written with Shravan K S from Indegene Limited. Enterprise AI is creating new opportunities for life sciences organizations to improve decision-making across commercial, medical, market access, and other business functions. But the quality of every AI model, dashboard, and business insight depends on one thing: trusted data. As enterprise data grows across multiple platforms, pipelines, and business domains, maintaining consistent data quality has become increasingly difficult. Manual data quality rule creation, fragmented governance, and evolving business definitions make it challenging to scale data quality across the enterprise. This post explores how Indegene built a production-grade, large language model (LLM) powered Data Quality Agent within its NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP) on AWS. The agent generates context-aware data quality rules, validates them, and produces ready-to-run SQL and Python code under centralized, human-in-the-loop governance. Together, these capabilities help organizations improve data quality at enterprise scale while reducing the effort required to build and maintain data quality programs. About Indegene Indegene Limited (BSE: 544172, NSE: INDGN) is the strategic operating partner to the life sciences industry, orchestrating commercial, medical, R&D, and safety operations across the product lifecycle. Trusted by the world’s top 20 biopharma companies, Indegene helps run complex, highly regulated workflows at global scale. Indegene combines deep life sciences expertise with AI-embedded platforms and governed operating models to improve speed, consistency, and compliance across mission-critical operations. By integrating technology into how work is executed and scaled, Indegene helps life sciences organizations deliver measurable outcomes in regulated environments. Why conventional data quality programs break down Most organizations have established data quality processes but keeping them effective is becoming increasingly difficult as enterprise data ecosystems evolve. One of the biggest challenges is the divide between technical and business rule ownership. Data engineers typically define technical rules that confirm whether data is structurally correct. For example, verifying that an HCP ID (Healthcare Professional ID) isn’t null, follows the required format, is unique, and maps to a valid reference record. Business teams define rules that determine whether the data makes sense in its operational context. For example, confirming that product market share totals 100 percent within a territory or that an HCP’s prescription activity aligns with their specialty and eligibility criteria. Because technical rules are often maintained in code while business rules reside in glossaries, SOPs, and subject-matter expertise, keeping them aligned and consistently governed across datasets and platforms becomes difficult. Traditional validation techniques also have inherent limitations. Checks for null values, data types, uniqueness, or referential integrity remain essential, but they can’t capture business-specific context. Validating product hierarchies, customer segmentation, territory alignment, or commercial business rules requires domain knowledge that static validation logic can’t easily represent. Creating and maintaining data quality rules is equally demanding. Every new dataset requires data profiling, rule definition, SQL development, validation, and ongoing maintenance. These rules are often spread across SQL scripts, pipeline code, spreadsheets, data catalogs, and tool-specific configurations. As schemas, business definitions, or validation thresholds change, the effort required to update and govern these rules grows significantly. Additionally, the operational impact is significant. Onboarding new datasets becomes slower because many activities are repeated manually. Maintaining quality rules across hundreds of datasets consumes valuable engineering effort. Business users lose confidence when validation rules are difficult to understand, trace, or relate to business context. As a result, data quality often becomes a periodic governance activity rather than a continuous, scalable capability. Rethinking data quality with generative AI Traditional data quality tools often operate as standalone capabilities, disconnected from the broader enterprise data ecosystem. As organizations scale AI and analytics, data quality needs to be embedded within the data platform itself, where governance, metadata, lineage, and analytics work together. Indegene addresses this through the NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP) , a modern, AI-driven data platform built specifically for life sciences. NEXT UDP brings together fragmented commercial, medical, clinical, and enterprise data into a single, governed environment so organizations can manage the complete data lifecycle from ingestion to analytics. NEXT UDP provides several standalone AI agents, such as the Data Ingestion agent, Data Quality agent, Orchestration agent, Data Catalog agent, and SQL Bot Generator agent. You can use them standalone within your data pipelines or customize them further for agent-to-agent communication. By integrating data ingestion, transformation, data quality, governance, metadata management, and analytics within a unified platform, NEXT UDP helps organizations: Consolidate fragmented enterprise data into a trusted source of truth. Standardize data quality and governance across business domains. Improve metadata visibility, lineage, and traceability. Reduce manual effort across data engineering workflows. Deliver trusted, AI-ready data for enterprise analytics and decision-making. items.title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity. When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer. Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories. In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. We then describe the security foundation beneath the platform, and close with a brief note on the spec-driven method the team used to build it. The problem: Too many systems, too much friction U Mobile’s IT landscape reflects the complexity typical of modern telecommunications: business support and customer relationship management systems, mobile number portability platforms, big data analytics, and infrastructure monitoring tools, running hybrid across on-premises and cloud. Before AiDaH, this fragmentation meant that even routine diagnoses required manually checking logs, querying subscriber eligibility, and consulting knowledge bases for business policies, across separate systems and portals. Each lookup was a context switch, each context switch was time lost, and each unresolved query became an escalation to a backend IT team. Expanding coverage to additional operational domains compounded the problem, because every new system typically required a bespoke integration. The ISD team’s strategy rested on three pillars. Reach : agents that coordinate across backend systems in real time. Depth : chain-of-thought reasoning for multi-step root cause analysis. Community : a secure multi-tenant framework with role-based access control and built-in guardrails, available to every division. The journey: From knowledge base to agentic platform AiDaH started with a principle: think big, start small. U Mobile began conceptualization in late 2025 with two pilot agents and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability. A Q1 2026 pilot brought the internal IT helpdesk online with 4 agents and 20 operational scenarios. Through 2026 the platform hardened and expanded, adding three-tier routing and reaching 6 agents by mid-year. AiDaH went live to 50 L2 call center and branch users in Q3 2026 with 8 agents, and now covers more than 150 documented operational scenarios. What agentic means in practice The difference between traditional AI assistance and agentic AI is best illustrated through a real example. With a traditional AI assistant, a support agent handling “mobile data not working overseas” gets help drafting a response and some suggested troubleshooting steps, but still manually checks roaming status, verifies eligibility, raises tickets, and sends the final reply. With AiDaH, the system independently checks the subscriber’s roaming configuration, verifies international data eligibility, and identifies the specific point of failure. It then assembles a remediation plan: which services to reset, what configuration to push, and whether a network ticket is warranted. The support agent reviews and confirms, and the actions execute. The investigation that used to consume the agent’s time now happens before they read the first line. The human decision point is preserved where it matters: at the moment something changes on a live subscriber account. In one production case, a subscriber reported being unable to purchase an add-on. AiDaH traced the failure to an error code, “Subscriber has pending order.” It also revealed that the customer had attempted the same purchase more than 30 times across multiple channels over three days, every attempt blocked by the same underlying pending order. AiDaH surfaced the root cause and the remediation steps in a single response. Previously that would have required manual investigation across several systems. Architecture: Six layers, one interface AiDaH runs on a layered architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, deployed in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region. items.title: See the agents, set the terms: new visibility and control for personal agents
items.description: Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site. Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business. See how agents access your site Knowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal agent traffic over time. In Top statistics, a new Personal Assistants widget lists which agents are visiting your site and how many requests each one sends. Filter on one agent and every other widget updates to show only its traffic details: the paths it requests, the status codes it receives, and the networks it comes from. At a glance, you can see whether an agent is logging in, reading your product pages, reaching your checkout, or hitting errors on pages it cannot use. For sites that protect user accounts with Account Abuse Protection (currently in early access), site owners and fraud teams are able to see which user each agent represents. The population overview page shows which personal agents are active across your users and how many accounts use them, so you can determine whether agent traffic is a meaningful part of your business. Every login and sign-up event now shows whether a personal agent made the request, and which one. Fraud teams can filter accounts by AI assistant events or number of AI assistants. Additionally, each user's account overview shows the agents acting for that account. A fraud analyst investigating an unusual login can tell whether it came from an agent the customer has relied on for weeks, or from an agent that appeared for the first time today and needs a closer look. If it looks like an attacker is using an agent on an account, fraud analysts can mitigate that account directly, with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID, without blocking the agent for everyone else who relies on it. Together, these views give you a clearer basis for deciding which personal agents to welcome, limit, or block. Set access policies that reflect your preferences We introduced AI bot policies this summer so site owners could make separate access control choices for AI bots used for Search, Training, and Agent behaviors. Now we’re expanding the existing Agents policy to include granular control options for supported personal agents. To reflect this broader scope, we’re renaming the setting AI Crawler and Agent access policies . In Security Settings , you can set an overall Agents policy, then choose a different policy for each supported personal agent: Allow (do not block) , Block on pages with ads , or Block . For example, you can set the overall Agents policy to Block on pages with ads , then choose Allow (do not block) for a supported personal agent you want to welcome. Your existing Search and Training policies stay as they are. You can also make these choices when you add a new zone to Cloudflare. During onboarding, we ask whether you monetize pages with ads and then tailor the recommended policies to your answer. You can always revisit your access controls later in Security Settings . The right policy depends on your site. One publisher may allow a supported personal agent throughout its site so readers can find its articles, while another may block that same agent on pages where ads support the content. Both publishers are choosing the access control that works for their business. Agent identity is only part of the story The analytics and policies we’re launching today give site owners visibility into personal agent activity and control over their access. Our next goal is to help site owners preserve the context of their relationships with users when personal agents act as intermediaries. A site may recognize the agent making a request but lack information it would otherwise have about the user: whether they are an existing customer, what they authorized the agent to do, whether they have a subscription, or which protections should apply. Reaching that goal will require privacy-aware ways to (1) carry user context through an agent, (2) help sites assess reputation, and (3) establish clear accountability when something goes wrong. We’ll be sharing more as we work with agent operators and others across the ecosystem, so site owners can choose whether to grant agents greater access while continuing to build relationships with their users. Make the choice for your site That person asking a personal agent to compare products, find support, or complete a purchase is still a customer trying to reach your business. Review how personal agents are accessing your site, then visit Security Settings → AI Crawler and Agent access policies to set the terms that work for your site.

items.title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
items.description: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem. Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

items.title: Desiderata for the Theory of Agents
items.description: TLDR: I give informal conceptual desiderata for the theory of agents we need to solve ASI alignment, and show a few examples of how existing theories fall short of these desiderata. A Theory of What? The word "agent" is often used in the AI safety discourse and in other research communities, but the intended meaning and scope of this concept varies substantially. For the purpose of this sequence, I informally define an agent to be a system with inputs ("observations") and outputs ("actions") that is effective at steering its environment in the direction of particular preferences, for a large variety of different environments. To do so, it arguably has to create a sophisticated model of the environment [1] , and use this model to build a long-term plan. Moreover, it has to continually update the model and revise the plan with new information and additional processing time. Additionally, it has to accomplish all of that while making efficient use of the available information (statistical efficiency) and computing resources (computational efficiency). The main examples of agents in the context of ASI alignment are (i) humans, and in particular users or stakeholders; (ii) the unaligned ASI we are trying to avoid or counteract; and (iii) the aligned ASI we are trying to create (such as the GDS ). Rocks, bacteria, and thermostats are non-examples: while a bacterium or a thermostat can be regarded as steering the environment, both are very limited in the variety of patterns in the environment they can exploit. For instance, if you switch the "cool" and "heat" outputs of a thermostat, it will not understand what has gone wrong and adapt its behavior. Animals and contemporary AIs are marginal cases (it's not obvious whether they should count). Given that agents are at the core of both the threat and the proposed solution, the theoretical foundation for ASI alignment requires a theory of agents. Now, concepts adjacent to "agent" have a considerable history of academic study, but different research communities approach the subject very differently—compare the frameworks used in decision theory (and, by extension, in game theory and economics), Hutter's " universal intelligence ", and reinforcement learning theory . It is therefore important to understand what the scope and level of abstraction of the theory of agents relevant for ASI alignment should be. To this end, I propose several desiderata. Descriptive The theory should be descriptive , i.e. applicable to all our main examples of agents. For any such example, the theory should ascribe specific preferences, beliefs, and any other alignment-relevant attributes to the agent [2] . These ascriptions should be grounded in the general philosophical soundness of the theory, not in domain knowledge about the specific examples; due to hypercomplexity , it is unlikely that domain knowledge will suffice [3] . In particular, if we imagine an alien civilization facing the AI alignment problem, or an AI agent facing the alignment problem for successor agents it wants to create, the theory should be about equally useful to them [4] . This means that agent theory should deconfuse us about philosophical questions pertaining to human preferences, such as, for example, the Caplan-Alexander debate on whether mental illness should be thought of as "unusual preferences". This doesn't mean that the answer to any particular question of this kind must be obvious from the theory, as it might come down to idiosyncratic nuances of the human brain. It does mean that if we also knew all pertinent facts about the physical world , we would be able to answer the question (or at least quantify the residual uncertainty), at least in principle. Actually inferring the answer from these facts might still be hard, just as explaining emergent physical phenomena can be hard even if all the relevant fundamental laws are known. On the other hand, descriptiveness doesn't require that concepts such as "human preferences" be perfectly unambiguous. It requires only that, to the extent they remain ambiguous, this ambiguity should not allow critical errors when Goodhart's Curse is accounted for. It is not obvious that these concepts can be made perfectly precise, but it is clear that the alignment problem is fundamentally normative (i.e. it is rooted in our preferring certain AI futures over other AI futures). When zooming in to a resolution at which our preferences are ill-defined, it becomes immaterial which choice to make, since our preferences are the only impetus for distinguishing these choices. Any imprecision that is inevitable is also tolerable. For example, imagine that Alice prefers to eat apples approximately 3 times as often as bananas, but there is no fully principled answer to the question "does Alice prefer to eat apples 2.99 times as often as bananas, or 3.01 times, or some number in the middle?" Then, it doesn't matter whether the AI aligned to Alice according to our theory will interpret her preference as 2.99 or 3.01—both are acceptable outcomes. In the mathematical formalism of the theory, this ambiguity might manifest as something like the choice of the universal Turing machine (UTM) in Solomonoff induction. Different UTMs correspond to priors that differ merely by a multiplicative constant, but for particular pairs of UTMs this constant can be arbitrarily large. Then, a reasonable choice might be any machine that we would intuitively consider "simple" or "natural". This doesn't nail down a single UTM, but might come close enough for the differences not to matter in practice [5] . This situation is not fundamentally different from that of most concepts in science. For example, astrophysicists find no difficulty discussing the "center of mass of the Sun", even though strictly speaking it is ill-defined: the boundary of the Sun is fuzzy, particle positions are only well-defined down to the scale of their Compton wavelength, and even the notion of space itself becomes ques

items.title: Schools that turn off Google's AI will lose search too starting in 2027
items.description: Starting in 2027, Google plans to turn off AI features in its school products by default, letting schools decide what to enable. The catch: schools that block AI entirely on their devices will also lose access to Google Search, since the two systems are now too deeply intertwined to separate. Given Google's grip on the US school market, that "choice" doesn't leave schools with much room to maneuver. The article Schools that turn off Google's AI will lose search too starting in 2027 appeared first on The Decoder .

items.title: Subquadratic Attention with a Hierarchical Tree-Structured Indexer
items.description: arXiv:2610.42112v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage of a billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million tokens of context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.

items.title: Li$^{2}$SAO: Lifting Light Single-Rollout Asynchronous RL Optimization via Group-Relative Actor-Critic Bootstrapping
items.description: arXiv:2610.40726v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) is becoming a mainstream paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), as it improves training efficiency by updating the model as rollouts arrive. Recent work argues that group-wise sampling in GRPO does not naturally fit asynchronous RL training because rollout lengths follow a long-tailed distribution, and proposes Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization (SAO) to improve stability and off-policy behavior, especially on agentic tasks. However, SAO relies on a closed-source value model obtained from scaling value pretraining. In this paper, we analyze GRPO and LiSAO, our lightweight reproduction of SAO without the pretrained value model, on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks. We find that GRPO outperforms LiSAO on reasoning tasks, while the reverse holds on agentic tasks. Since the value model of LiSAO is not yet well trained , LiSAO lags behind GRPO substantially in early training steps. To address this issue, we propose Li$^{2}$SAO, which Lifts Light Single-rollout Asynchronous Optimization with group-relative actor-critic bootstrapping: while the critic is cold, a group-relative advantage trains the actor and a group-centered return trains the critic, after which training switches to single-rollout GAE. Experiments show that Li$^{2}$SAO catches up with or surpasses GRPO in early training and further raises the later performance ceiling. Code is available at https://github.com/jd-cc-coder/Li2SAO.

items.title: PsyInterviewee: Informational Invariance and Relational Adaptivity in Mental Health Interview Simulation
items.description: arXiv:2610.41289v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-based simulated interviewees support interviewer training and the evaluation of mental health interviewing systems. Existing studies have primarily focused on improving human-likeness through richer patient profiles and behavioral modeling. However, human-likeness alone does not establish their reliability. Reliable simulation requires preserving profile-grounded clinical facts (informational invariance) while adapting disclosure and interaction behavior to the interview (relational adaptivity). To this end, we introduce PsyInterviewee, which separates a protected truth channel from a dynamic interaction channel and verifies generated clinical claims against the profile. Specifically, asymmetric write permissions allow dialogue context to update disclosure and behavioral states without authorizing new clinical facts; these states guide what profile-supported information is revealed and how it is expressed. In an automated evaluation of interactions between LLM-based interviewers and interviewees, PsyInterviewee achieves higher scores than four representative baselines on most metrics across both axes, as assessed by two LLM judges. Ablations suggest that the two channels contribute to clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.

items.title: Enhancing Knowledge Entity Relation Extraction in Abstracts and Full-text Content of Academic Articles Using Large Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.41552v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.

items.title: Keepace.ai: A Technical Report on a Large Language Model for Sports and Health
items.description: arXiv:2610.38249v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models hold promise for delivering safe, scientifically grounded, and personalized exercise guidance at scale, yet the sports-and-health domain still lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Keepace (Keepace.ai) is a domain-specialized LLM built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across three tasks: workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, Keepace outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy. This report summarizes the current design, data pipeline, safety-first evaluation framework, and evaluation results of Keepace.

items.title: Beyond fabrication: Misattributed numbers in papers written by AI research agents
items.description: arXiv:2610.38691v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Verifying numerical claims in research written by AI agents is an important but challenging problem. Recent benchmarks show that many agent-written papers fail integrity checks, but such verdicts, often produced by a single LLM judge, identify failure without explaining its nature, and existing checks either test a paper for internal consistency or test whether a reported value appears somewhere in an agent's output. We re-analyze all 540 released judgments from a recent public benchmark of AI research agents (nine agents, fifteen open research problems) and manually label 256 numerical claims from 18 submissions. Failures concentrate on alignment between the paper and the underlying work rather than overt cheating, and about four in five unsupported claims correspond to values in the agent's own files that come from the wrong experiment, metric, or run. We introduce a deterministic claim-to-evidence checker that scores whether the surrounding context identifies the claimed result and calibrates each claim against numerical decoys. With its rules fixed before labeling, it certifies claims with over 90% precision against blinded annotators (78 of 85; Cohen's kappa = 0.89), while verifying only a subset of claims; most claims it cannot verify are nevertheless traceable, so failure to verify is not evidence of falsehood. An LLM verifier given the same evidence recovers more traceable claims but accepts about three times as many misattributed ones, so the two are best used together. Applied to 99 submissions, the checker reveals large differences in traceability across agents, and on 30 submissions a second judge configuration, with a different model and harness, orders the agents' vendor groups as the official judge does while passing twice as many papers. These findings motivate provenance-first auditing of AI-produced research.

items.title: Efficient Agentic Audio-Visual Question Answering through Toolset Pruning and Modality Consolidation
items.description: arXiv:2610.38960v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fine-grained audio-visual question answering (AVQA) requires models to resolve complex cross-modal correspondences and temporally grounding from sparsely distributed evidence. Omni-modal agents, which autonomously orchestrate perception tools to actively collect evidence, achieve strong performance, but it remains unclear whether active perception from both audio and visual modalities depends on broad specialized toolsets, especially audio or visual modality-specific tools. Such systems may also introduce long execution trajectories and substantial inference cost. We investigate whether comparable performance can be retained with a compact workflow exposing only essential perceptual capabilities. Starting from the specialized-tool OmniAgent, we conduct staged controlled experiments that prune the toolset and progressively consolidate modality-specific tools into omni-modal tools, motivating a two-tool agent comprising only Omni-modal captioning and Omni-modal QA. Across three widely used AVQA benchmarks, our compact agent achieves comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent while reducing inference cost by around 70%.

items.title: Rank-Aware Differentially Private Release of Listwise Preferences for LLM Alignment
items.description: arXiv:2610.37682v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Listwise preference feedback offers richer supervision for large language model (LLMs) alignment than pairwise comparisons, but a full ranking also reveals more sensitive user preferences. Existing privacy-preserving alignment methods focus mainly on pairwise feedback, while listwise alignment under local differential privacy (LDP) remains unexplored. Extending LDP to this listwise domain raises a critical challenge: the high sensitivity of the full ranking space demands excessive noise, neutralizing the benefits of listwise supervision. To address this challenge, we analyze the interaction between supervision granularity and privacy noise in downstream training, and introduce a rank-aware exponential mechanism that privatizes listwise preference data into a low-sensitivity granularity suitable for downstream alignment. The mechanism leverages ranking information to sample a fixed-size binary partition, concentrating the noise near borderline items instead of perturbing all items uniformly as randomized response (RR) does. Empirical evaluations on downstream LLM alignment tasks show that our mechanism consistently outperforms existing LDP baselines at matched privacy budgets. The code is available at https://github.com/tdsai-lab/RAEM.

items.title: T2D: Target-to-Draft Model Pruning & Adaptation for Efficient Speculative Decoding
items.description: arXiv:2610.34103v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speculative decoding significantly accelerates autoregressive text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), but its efficacy depends largely on two key factors: the distributional alignment between the draft and the target model, and the draft model's latency during inference. However, existing approaches typically utilize independently pretrained small draft models or seek to prune the target model to a manually chosen architecture, thereby failing to explicitly balance the trade-off between draft model alignment and token generation efficiency. To address this gap, we formulate draft model design as an optimization problem and propose T2D, a framework that constructs draft models directly from the target model using latency-aware structured pruning and knowledge distillation. In this manner, T2D obtains draft models that are jointly optimized for both measured inference latency and cross-entropy loss on the target model's responses, resulting in superlative speculative decoding performance. Through extensive experiments on multi-domain speculative decoding benchmarks and across several target model families of differing scale, we demonstrate how T2D prunes up to 92\% of the target model to obtain highly performant draft models compared to competitive baselines. Moreover, draft models obtained via T2D can also be utilized by other speculative decoding token-alignment and knowledge distillation methods in a plug-and-play fashion, leading to further gains. Our findings underscore the importance of jointly navigating the draft model architecture-alignment frontier to unlock the full potential of speculative decoding for LLMs.

items.title: 製造業の「秘伝のタレ」はAIに奪われるのか、競争力の源泉はどこにある？
items.description: ヤマザキマザックは「JIMTOF2026」において、ブース内セミナーを開催。本稿では、その中で政策研究大学院大学 特任教授の西垣淳子氏と、ヤマザキマザック 上席執行役員 商品開発本部 副本部長の澤田洋祐氏が行った「製造業の『秘伝のタレ』はどこにあるのか？」の内容を紹介する。

items.title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings
items.description: arXiv:2611.00172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embedding models underpin virtually every modern AI system, from search engines to recommendation systems. Despite shared mathematical foundations, research on embedding models remains fragmented by modality: the communities develop largely in isolation, seldom exchanging insights. We argue that this fragmentation obscures a deeper convergence. Driven by contrastive learning, Transformer architectures, and a granularity shift, embedding research across modalities is converging toward a common set of principles, even as modality-specific challenges remain underexplored. To reason across this convergence without conflating it, we propose a framework of three progressively harder capabilities: coverage, comparability, and compositionality. Three paths toward unification satisfy these in turn: transformation broadens coverage, alignment enables comparability, and joint embedding, the terminus we advocate, aims at compositionality. This position paper traces the resulting evolution, providing the first unified, cross-cutting treatment of omnimodal embedding research.

items.title: MEMENTO: Learning Context Management for Long Context Processing Agents
items.description: arXiv:2611.00244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents that operate over long inputs must perform context management: deciding what to retain in a fixed-size context window. A common approach is compaction, where the model replaces its history with a self-generated note. Yet off-the-shelf agentic models, including GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.3, often write ineffective notes, and reinforcement learning (RL) alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior. We present MEMENTO, a long-context agent built on Qwen3-8B and trained to manage its context through compaction. We first bootstrap note-taking by fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforce it with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics, and confidence calibration. Although trained only to compact into a fresh window, MEMENTO extends at test time to strategies such as context folding and confidence-based backtracking. On book-level question answering across four benchmarks, with books of up to 2.5M tokens, MEMENTO raises Qwen3-8B's accuracy from 36.9% to 67.8% while never holding more than 20K tokens in context. It outperforms GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost. It also nearly matches a ~100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost, and comes within 6.4 points of GLM-5.3 full context at 1/26 the cost.

items.title: Cross-Lingual Persona Effects in LLM Negotiation
items.description: arXiv:2611.00300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tell an LLM negotiator to be "headstrong" and it should hold firm on price, but does that instruction retain the same behavior in every language? To test this, we use identical buyer and seller instances of Gemini 3.6 Flash to negotiate the same 12 CraigslistBargain scenarios in English and Korean. The pilot-scale 2 x 2 x 3 design crosses interaction language, seller urgency (none or strong), and buyer persona (cooperative, neutral, or headstrong), yielding 432 attempted negotiations. We call this property cross-lingual social-policy fidelity: whether a prompt-defined social policy produces the same behavioral effect regardless of interaction language. It often does not. Korean negotiations reached agreement far more often than English (77.3% vs. 52.5%, a 24.8-point gap, Holm-adjusted p = .0039), but only for neutral and headstrong buyers; cooperative buyers were already near-ceiling in both languages. Buyers' opening offers barely differed by language; the gap instead emerged later, through larger seller concessions and a smaller final gap in Korean, and agreed prices were also lower in Korean. Repeating the full design with Qwen3.7 Flash as both agents gives directional support: agreement was again higher in Korean (+13.9 points vs. Gemini's +24.8, with an interval whose lower bound is near zero), and sellers again conceded more. Pragmatic analysis reveals why: while both languages frequently featured face-threatening acts like rejections and counter-offers, Korean dialogue softened these threats with substantially more politeness mitigation, especially among sellers (11.7% vs. 3.6%). These results show that such a policy can produce different simulated negotiation behavior, not just different wording, when only the interaction language changes.

items.title: GAVAGAI: Referential Alignment for Infant-Scale Vision-Language Models via Balanced Optimal Transport
items.description: arXiv:2611.00319v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A child learns which words name which things from roughly 100 million words of input. Vision-language models trained at a comparable scale bind words to referents far less reliably, and we argue that part of the gap is structural: the usual next-token captioning objective has no variable standing for "this word refers to that region," so training applies no direct pressure to ground words. We add such a variable by treating each scene as a small assignment problem between the content words heard and the regions seen, solved as entropic optimal transport under two constraints. First, a word may be assigned to a special NOTHING column instead of any region, which matters because most content words in caregiver speech do not name anything visible. Second, no region may receive more than a bounded share of the assignment mass, a capacity constraint that encodes mutual exclusivity. The alignment step costs about eight Sinkhorn iterations, small next to the vision encoder. In controlled simulation, the naive version of the idea, a row-wise softmax that forces every word onto some region, collapses to 0.000 word-to-picture accuracy under realistic non-reference rates, below the 0.058 of captioning alone, while our two constraints reach 0.075 in that regime and 0.700 on clean input. A one-parameter version of the model reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy across three ambiguity conditions (RMSE 0.024). On the SAYCam infant video corpus, adding the alignment loss to a next-token captioning model raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38. A contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark, so our claim is that the loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, not that it sets a new best.

items.title: Queering the Audits: Community-Based Auditing of AI Harms to Queer Communities
items.description: arXiv:2611.00345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems embed majority-group defaults into training data, evaluation metrics, and category definitions, producing documented harms for queer communities including erasure, misclassification, and discrimination. Standard technical audits often rely on aggregate measures and cannot detect harms that be come visible only through the lived experience of affected communities. We conducted a participatory auditing workshop at EurIPS 2025 where 16 queer community members audited four case studies using the 4Cs harm taxonomy (Content, Conduct, Contact, Contract) applied across the AI lifecycle. Participants used structured worksheets and plenary synthesis to classify harms and trace them to their origins in the development pipeline. Across all four cases, participants traced harms to problem definition and data collection, and they identified contractual structures that extract value from vulnerable populations while providing minimal recourse. These findings illustrate that community-informed auditing surfaces concrete, identity-specific harms that aggregate evaluation methods risk overlooking.

items.title: Cross-Prompt Reuse of Entity-Replacement Responses
items.description: arXiv:2611.00352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With model weights fixed, we measure how much of an entity-replacement response transfers between English factual questions, beyond whether answers change. We add the hidden-state change from two source questions to a target question about the same entity, comparing the predicted log-probability shift between two relations' published answers, given known answer prefixes, with the measured one. Hidden reuse injects the aligned change at 50% depth before the target's remaining layers; direct reuse adds source output-score changes. With other-relation sources, hidden reuse removes 45% and 49% of no-change error on 0.5-1B Qwen and Llama. Gemma-2-2B removes 22% and passes one of three comparisons in plain text without its default beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token. A later protocol restoring it yields 58-68%, passing every comparison on three cohorts. Larger checkpoints, chat format and new entities show replication and format- or cohort-dependent failures. On small plain-format checkpoints, other-relation hidden reuse mainly reproduces the shift both relations' questions share, without reliably lowering relation-selective error. With target-relation sources, hidden reuse's post hoc advantage over direct reuse is 0.2-0.9 nats outside chat format, unconfirmed and not replacement-specific. The same relation-neutral change at both questions' entity tokens lowers relation-selective error more than random or other-replacement changes, indicating receiving-question dependence.

items.title: Humanized but Still True? Auditing Facts and Detection in AI-Text Humanizers
items.description: arXiv:2611.00359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI "humanizers" rewrite machine-generated text so that detectors classify it as human-written. Public leaderboards score evasion and embedding similarity, but not whether checkable details survive. We check whether numbers, dates, person and organization names, and quoted spans survive each rewrite, using a rule-based checker validated by two AI annotators (precision 0.84-1.00, recall 0.93-0.95; no human annotation). In the October 2026 cycle of a public humanizer leaderboard, all 11 commercial tools changed or dropped at least one of these units in 35-65% of the documents that contained one. Most changes were to quoted spans; counting numbers and names alone, 10 of the 11 tools still altered at least one in 20% or more of the documents. The September 2026 cycle was similar (19-50%).
